COTTON CLEARING HOUSE.
Want to Do Their Own Banking Business.
devising a plan whereby cotton contracts for future delivery can be cleared at once without waiting for the time of delivery to arrive; in other words, to prepare and present to the board of managers and members of the exchange a modern clearing house system for such contracts. The committee, it was learned, consists of Daniel O'Dell chairman; Charles W. Ide, Paul S. Galatti, John A. Cartcorn, Jr., and Edward S. Coott.

The proposition to inaugurate a new system of clearances has been talked over for some time by members and officials of the exchange, and early last fall the matter assumed definite shape when Thomas M. Robinson, who was then president, was authorized by the managers, at the request of several prominent members to name a committee of five to "investigate and report to the exchange for subsequent consideration and action, the practicability and advisability of the adoption of such a system, and if in their judgment found advisable, to prepare a plan which to them shall seem most desirable to that end,' although that committee spent much time, no conclusions were reached up to the time of the annual election of the officers of the exchange. The board of managers, however, were in favoring of continuing the investigation and President-Hubbard was accordingly authorized to appoint a new committee, the members of which are now announced.

The appointment of this committee revives interest in a proposition that is of much importance to members of the cotton exchange, although there is still a wide difference of opinion among them as to the successful outcome of the undertaking. There is a very large element in the exchange that strongly supports the proposition itself and believes it possible to devise a satisfactory working plan for the immediate clearance or future contracts. There are not a few members, on the other hand, who are unqualifiedly opposed to the principle itself, and will probably not support the movement, although much depends, of course, upon what plan the committee may ultimately decide upon.
In speaking of the matter, Chairman O'Dell said that, in his opinion there was no reason why a clearing house system could not be made for the New York Cotton Exchange, for the immediate clearing of contracts for future delivery. He thought that such a system would undoubtedly benefit the market and increase the trade and possibly membership.

TEN DOLLAR
BILL MISSING
YOUNG MAN FROM THE COUNTRY MEETS USUAL FATE IN THE TENDERLOIN.
HACK DRIVERS DID
NOT NEED A LICENSE.
Were Driving for Private Patrons— Molly Murray Had a Noisy Circus Jag.
Judge Sullivan this morning had another of those cases before him that would require the wisdom of a Solomon to decide.

J. S. England, a young man from the country, came to town yesterday, and last night went out to see the sights. He says he wandered into Lizzie Hill's place at 36, East Galena, bought a round of drinks and then went out to supper. When he came to pay he found that a $10 bill was missing, and thereupon returned to Lizzie's and taxed her with the theft.

On her part, the woman said England exhibited his money when he left her place, which was admitted by the complainant. She insisted he went to other places after leaving and this he denied.

The court fined the woman $15.

Billy Berkley, charged with beating Alex O'Bannon, a colored man, pleaded guilty and was fined $15. This exonerates Steve Hoy, who was first implicated, as he had nothing to do with the affair.

Two hack drivers arrested yesterday for running hacks without numbers or licenses, were discharged. It appeared that the vehicles belonged to livery stables and were not operated on the street, being simply closed carriages that were sent for by patrons.

G. M. Lewis, charged with cruelty to animals, pleaded not guilty and will be tried on Tuesday.

Molly Murray, a colored woman who has long been a somewhat picturesque figure on Galena alley, succumbed to the circus. She was discharged yesterday, a charge of vagrancy failing to stick and went to the tent show last night to celebrate. After the show the celebration continued, and this morning was still going on at full blast. Then Molly loaded up with a fresh charge of squirrel whisky and started out to climb telegraph poles. Officer Elderkin undertook the unpleasant task of bringing her to the police station, and on the way up she entertained the populace with a highly original skirt dance, interspersed with vocal selections. Molly admitted that she was drunk, "good and drunk too," but indignantly denied that she had disturbed the peace and demanded trial. She will get it tomorrow.

boston-frederick-1900-08-09.A1:
NEGRO SLAIN BY THE POSSE.
Escaped Convict Resisted Arrest and Is Shot Down.
FAIRBURN, Ga., Aug. 9. — Boston Frederick, a negro of desperate character and an escaped convict, has been killed in the lower part of this county by a posse of citizens, led by a deputy sheriff, who were trying to effect his capture.

Frederick was indicted by the grand jury February, 1899, for arson, being implicated in the burning of Palmetto. This bill was quashed, but the negro was sent to the chaingang for 12 months for carrying concealed weapons. He served this sentence out and returned to this county, and was soon again sent up for another 12 months for assault and battery. It was while serving this sentence in the employment of A. G. Orvin & Co. of South Georgia that he escaped and returned to this county, and he has been swearing vengeance on everybody who had anything to do with his several convictions.

Sheriff Aderhold received a message from parties near where the negro was in hiding, asking him to come and arrest the negro. He directed that a deputy summon a posse and make the arrest.

When the posse came up with the negro he leveled a doublebarreled shotgun at them, and was instantly shot down.
boston-frederick-1900-08-09.A2:
Negro Killed by Officers
Fairburn, Ga., Aug. 9.—Boston Frederick, colored, was killed in the lower part of this county yesterday by a posse of citizens led by a deputy sheriff, who were trying to effect his capture. Frederick was indicted by the grand jury February, 1899.
boston-frederick-1900-08-09.A3:
Killed Fugitive Convict.
While resisting arrest Wednesday afternoon late, Boston Frederick, a desperate negro, escaped from the chaingang, at Fairburn, several weeks ago, was killed by the deputy sheriff of Campbell county and a posse near that place. Frederick was indicted by the grand jury last year for arson, the charge being that he was implicated in the burning of Palmetto. The bill was quashed, but he was sent up for carrying concealed weapons. His presence in the county was known and an effort was made to arrest him. He levelled a gun on the officer and posse and was fired upon and instantly killed.

canny-clark-dade-city-1900-07-31.A1:
Killed a Desperado.
Sheriff H. C. Griffin and posse killed a negro desperado. Canny Clark, at daybreak Tuesday, near the turpentine camp of Allison & Gasque, not far from Dade City. By chance the posse met the negro on the road. Clark immediately drew his revolver and attempted to shoot the sheriff. The posse riddled him with buckshot. At the inquest the verdict was justifiable homicide.

coot-miles-phoenix-city-1900-08-09.A1:
NEGRO FATALLY WOUNDED
Ran from the Officers and Was Shot Down
Columbus, Ga., August 9.—(Special.)— "Coot" Miles, a negro, was fatally shot in Phoenix City, Ala., today by Policeman John Moon. The negro was wanted on three warrants in Phoenix City and Girard, one of them grand larceny. It is said he threatened the life of Phoenix and Girard officers and carried a gun for them. When Officer Moon saw the negro he started to arrest him, and the negro ran. The officer gave chase, firing as he went. The fifth shot struck the negro, and he darted into a ravine near by, where the officer found him, shot through the lung and probably mortally wounded. Miles was still lingering tonight. He was 175 yards from the officers when hit.
coot-miles-phoenix-city-1900-08-09.A2:
DESPERADO FATALLY SHOT.
Policeman Fired the Shot While Trying to Arrest Him.
Policeman Fired the Shot While Trying to Arrest Him.

Columbus, Ga., Aug. 9.—Coot Miles, a negro desperado, was fatally shot in Phenix City to-day by Policeman John Moon, the negro was wanted on three warrants in Phenix City and Girard, one of them for grand larceny. It is said that he threatened the life of Phenix and Girard officers, and had carried a gun for them.

When Officer Moon saw the negro he started to arrest him, and the negro ran. The officer gave chase, firing as he went. The fifth shot struck the negro, and he darted into a ravine nearby, where the officer found him shot through the lung, and probably mortally wounded.

Miles was still living to-night. He was one hundred and seventy-five yards from the officer when hit. Moon used a big Colt's revolver. Miles is the son of a negro desperado, who recently escaped from Phenix City officers.

TEXAS.
Lumber Trade on the Increase.
Unprecedented Fall Of Rain.

The present season at Brenham is said to be the worst in years. There has been an unprecedented rainfall in that section recently which hasn't its equal in the remembrance of the oldest inhabitant.

Princeton Man to Coach.

Thompson, the Princeton coach, has been selected to coach the football team of the University of Texas at Austin this season. Practice on the team will commence September 25.

Deputy Marshal Killed.

United States deputy marshal Goddard was killed Tuesday night near Goldwater, on the lower edge of the Choctaw nation, by an Indian whom he was attempting to arrest on a charge of murder.

valuable Buffalo Dead.

Two of the buffalo from Goodnight's ranch died at Sherman this week. They had been on exhibition there by "Buffalo" Jones. The two animals were among the few buffalo left in the country, and were valued at more than $1000.

Sheriff Foils a Mob.

A mob of enraged citizens at Longview, Texas, organized a mob a few nights ago for the purpose of lynching John Dickson, a negro charged with attempted assault on a young white girl. Sheriff Howard learned of the plans of the mob, and had the negro removed to the county jail at Marshall.

Two Crops From One Field.

The farmers of Denton county will make two crops this year off the same land, one of wheat and the other of cotton. The rains of June and July are responsible for the unusual success. From twenty to twenty-five bushels of wheat and half a bale of cotton per acre is the average.

Machinery Removes a Finger.

Robert Landrum, a young boy employet at the Diamond rolling mills at Taylor, while working around the gearing of a grain elevator got his hand caught in the machinery, and before assistance could reach him one finger was cut completely off.

Greatest Texas Art Exhibit.

Among the features of the international fair of San Antonio which will open October 20, will be one of the largest and best art exhibits ever got together in Texas. Lee A. Adams is superintendent of the art department of the fair.

Rice Land Leased.
Four thousand acres of land in the Braman tract was leased yesterday for rice culture. A big company is back of the deal. A canal will be built, and the company next year will put two thousand acres in rice. The land is located in Matagorda county, west of the Colorado.

Negro Colns Money.

A negro claiming to have come from Anderson county, was caught in Grosbeck recently. selling the questions and answers to the applicants for certificates. He coined money for a time at the rate of $10 per applicant. As a result the entire set of questions was thrown aside and new ones made for the examinations.

Killed At a Pasture Gate.

N. A. Sheffield, of Milam county, was shot while trying to open the gate to a pasture five miles from Kennedy, last Friday night. He was driving with his wife in a buggy, and had gotten out to open the gate when the fatal shots were fired. The trail of the murderers was followed for some distance, but finally lost, and no arrests have been made.

Prominent Stockman Killed.

Joe Earp, a well known stockman, was killed by his brother-in-law, W. C. Chapman, at the home of the latter at Waldo, last week. It is claimed that Earp drew a knife on Chapman and that the latter shot in self defence. Chapman surrendered immediately after the shooting, to constable Frank Harring.

State Normal Board.

The summer normal board of examiners at Austin has finished its work of grading the examination papers of all applicants for certificates in the 116 normals in the state this summer. Thirty-two colored and seventy-five white took the examinations. Forty-five per cent of the negroes and seventy-three per cent of the whites received certificates.

ANOTHER ACCOUNT.
(Special Dispatch to The Times.)
LYNCHBURG. VA. August 8.—N
(Special Dispatch to The Times.)

LYNCHBURG, VA., August 8.—News reached here to-day of a sensational shooting affair near Pedlar Mills, in Amherst county, and from all accounts it almost rivals the recent events in New Orleans. A negro named Smith, a son of Paul Smith, it seems, was wanted on a warrant, and owing to threats that he is said to have made, Constable Martin in going to make the arrest took with him a posse of eight men.

BREECH LOADER.

They went to the negro's house Tuesday night, and found him waiting for them with a breech loading shot-gun. The negro shot a number of times, wounding five of the posse. Mr. Thomas Carter, one of the posse, is said to be seriously injured.

The wounds of the others are not dangerous. It is stated that the negro has been arrested. Full details of the affair have not been obtained, as Pedlar is several miles from any railroad or telegraph station.
paul-smith-pleasant-view-1900-08-07.A4:
OTHER SIDE OF STORY.
he statement made by the negro
OTHER SIDE OF STORY.
The statement made by the negroes is that the Martins attacked them in the afternoon, and that night when Constable Carter and his posse came up they opened fire on their house without saying a word. Sentiment seems somewhat divided among the white people in regard to the matter. The prisoners were taken to Lynchburg to-day for safe keeping where they will be kept until court day. The prisoners have employed A. E. Strode as their attorney.
paul-smith-pleasant-view-1900-08-07.A5:
SHERIFF BEARD
TELLS THE STORY
Shooting of the Posse of Eight Men in Amherst.
YOUNG NEGROES DID SHOOTING.
The Trouble Commenced in the Quarantining of a Colored Church,
When the Posse Called on the Negroes They Fired.
(Special Dispatch to The Times.)
AMHERST, VA. August 9-The foll

AMHERST, VA., August 9.—The following is a statement made by Deputy Sheriff A. D. Beard, who brought the four negro men here last night charged with the shooting of Constable Carter and others, near-Pleasant View, on Tuesday night: I arrived at Pleasant View yesterday about noon and found that the negroes had given themselves up to Justice R. C. Wilcher, upon the condition that they would be protected from the hands of a mob."

At the preliminary hearing before Justice Wilcher there were about seventy-five white men and twenty or twenty-five negroes in attendance. I found excitement running high, and as soon as I could get the papers fixed up by the Justice I hastened off for the court-house where I landed safely with my four prisoners about 8 o'clock in the evening.

QUARANTINED A CHURCH.

The quarrel seems to have grown out of quarantining the colored church, in which an association was being held, as there had been some smallpox in that neighborhood and this action was ordered by the Board of Health. These negroes became very much infuriated over their church being closed and seemed to lay the blame on Constable Wm. Martin, their adjoining farmer, who had posted the notice on the church door.

On Tuesday evening the young negroes and the Martins, had a row, in which it is stated that both sides did some reckless firing, but none of the shots took effect.

WARRANTS SWORN OUT.

The Martins immediately swore out warrants for the arrest of these negroes, and T. J. Carter was made special constable, as Martin, who was involved in the difficulty, was the regular officer.

Constable Carter summoned seven men to assist him, and proceeded to the house of Paul Smith, the father of these boys and called them out two or three times. The negroes made no reply, but raised their windows and fired into the crowd a number of times, wounding all eight of them, three perhaps seriously, the others very slightly. Paul Smith, the father of these boys, is a hard working,well behaved, thrifty negro, who has accumulated some property.
paul-smith-pleasant-view-1900-08-07.A7:
The injuries of William Carter are very serious and his condition is not favorable.

The negroes had a hearing before Magistrate Wilisher and were sent on to the grand jury. A few days ago the health board of Pedlar's district, on account of smallpox, passed a resolution directing the negroes of the neighborhood not to hold a certain church festival. A notice to that effect was placed on the church. It was torn down, so it is stated, by one of the Smith boys, and it is said that the same young man had a difficulty with Constable Martin, who swore out a warrant for his arrest.

FIFTY SHOTS

The posse went to the Smith home at about one o'clock Wed esday morning and about fifty shots were exchanged by the officers and negroes. The shooting on the part of the negroes was done by two of the negro boys, who were stationed behind a chicken coop with a single barreled breechloader and an old pistol. Every member of the posse was wounded.

The affair created intense excitement, and before morning people began assembling at the house, thus giving the officers immense reinforcements.

THE SUKRENDER.

The Smiths finally consented to surrender, it being understood that they were not to be lynched and were to have a fair trial. Sheriff Beard thought it advisable to bring them here. In a statement made to your correspondent this afternoon, the negroes claimed that they did not know that the posse had a warrant for their arrest, but were under the impression that they were a gang of white cappers.
paul-smith-pleasant-view-1900-08-07.A8:
NINE MEN WOUNDED.
FIGHT BETWEEN CONSTABLE'S POSSE AND NEGROES.
Amherst C. H., Va., Aug. 9.—Constable T. J. Carter, with a posse, attempted to arrest a number of negroes in the house of Paul Smith, near Pleasant View, in this county, last night, and as a result every one of the force was wounded—three seriously, and Paul Smith, his two sons, and his nephew are here in jail to-night. One of the negroes is slightly wounded.

There had been trouble the evening before between Constable Martin and the Smith family, and in this difficulty several shots were exchanged. As Constable Martin was one of the parties to this difficulty Justice R. C. Wilsher deemed it expedient to appoint a special constable to arrest the Smiths. T. J. Carter was appointed, and with his posse, proceeded to the house of Paul Smith. The Smith family refused to surrender, and instead of obeying the mandate of the constable, opened fire upon that officer and his posse.

There are two versions of the trouble, the negroes claiming that the white men fired upon them first, and the other side that the negroes opened fire first, as above stated.

The wounded are T. J. Carter and brother, two of the Martin brothers, Abner Franklin, John L. Sale, Myers and one whose name could not be ascertained.

After the shooting Paul Smith came out of the house and gave himself up, asking protection, and the other members of the family were also arrested.

An examination was had to-day before Colonel R. C. Wilsher, with a large crowd of whites drawn up on one side of the road and blacks on the other, and for awhile excitement ran high, and further and serious trouble seemed imminent. But wiser counsels prevailed and the negroes were lodged safely in jail here to-night. At this writing everything is quiet and no further trouble is expected. The Smith family had four guns and a pistol, all of which were emptied before they were captured.

The women quickly spread and Capt. Jesse T. Capt Wade fell mortally wounded The pose withdrew and went for sheriff Thompson. The sheriff, with a re-enforced pose, is now in pursuit. In the section where the tragedy occurred the colored population considerably outnumber the white, and the information is that the cooled neighbors of the Alexander will assist them in resisting the sheriff. The absurdity of this proposition is emphasized by his present condition. A special constable is "as far away" from a legal one as it is possible for a man to be. (Special Dispatch to The Times.)

LYNCURBURG YA. August 17 - I

LYNCHBURG, VA., August 17.—Judge Stafford G. Whittle, of the Circuit Court, sent here to-day his opinion in the case of the Lynchburg Electric Railway and Light Company vs. the city of Lynchburg. The object of the suit was to secure an injunction to restrain the city from carrying out the ordinance regulating the use of electric poles and wires.

In his opinion Judge Whittle grants the injunction on the ground that the City Council had no right to relegate governmental power to the Electrical Board and the city electrician. An appeal will be taken from Judge Whittle's decision, and in the meantime the city electrician will be a functionary without a vestige of power to act.

The negro Paul Smith and his sons, Walter, Ellis and Wilson, who are charged with shooting and wounding all of a posse of eight men sent to arrest one of them, will be taken to Amherst Courthouse on Monday for trial. The men who were wounded are doing well, and the three who were seriously injured are entirely out of danger.
paul-smith-pleasant-view-1900-08-07.A15:
Forty-one Indictments.
Lynchburg, Va., Aug. 24.—Forty-one indictments have been found against the five negroes, Paul Smith and his three sons, Wilson, Ellis and Creed Smith, and Nelson Smith, who are charged with shooting and wounding all of the members of the posse of eight men who went to arrest one of them near Pedlar's, in Amherst county, a few days ago. In the trial the Commonwealth's Attorney of Amherst will be assisted by B. T. Gordon, Commonwealth's Attorney of Nelson, and Mr. W. K. Allen, of Amherst.

Two Men Suffocated.

George Hudgins and Ike Chandler met a tragic death in a well at Hot Springs. The men were digging the well, and had gone down about 25 feet. Hudgins was at the bottom and Chandler was using the windlass to raise the dirt. Suddenly Chandler heard a cry for help and he immediately descended to rescue Hudgins, who was dying from suffocation. When Chandler reached the bottom he, too, was overcome by suffocation and called to those at the windlass to pull him up. He was hauled near the top in a dazed condition and fell back, breaking his neck. The dead bodies of both men were then drawn from the well with hooks.

Unknown Man Murdered.

A man who gave his name as Griffith was found in a semi-conscious condition in the suburbs of Pine Bluff, his head beaten almost to a jelly. On his person was found a ticket from Pine Bluff to Camden and return. He was unable to give an account of how he became in such condition, but managed to state that he was enroute to El Dorado to visit a son. The police are of the opinion that the man was knocked off a train and robbed. He is about 39 years old, small black moustache, and partially bald.

Weather Report.

The weather report for Arkansas week ending August 22d, shows tha excessively hot and dry weather prevailed. Light scattered showers occurred in a few localities, but was not of much benefit to growing crops. Cotton has suffered to a great extent, the hot, dry weather causing it to wilt and shed rapidly. It has commenced to open in some localities. Late corn is badly injured and in some places will be a total failure. The thrashing of wheat and oats continues, and the yield is fair to good.

Used a Hatchet.

Capt. W. W. Early, a one-armed ex Confederate, had a narrow escape from death at the hands of a colored woman in Fort Smith. Alice Johnton is the woman's name. She had been working for Mr. Early's family and went to the House in an intoxicated condition. When Early remonstrated with her she flew at him with a hatchet, striking him a blow in the head, inflicting an ugly wound. Just as she was in the act of striking her victim the second time a neighbor grabbed her arm and wrenched the weapon from her, thus saving Mr. Early's life.

Found Dead In the Road.

James T. Venable, manager of a sawmill near England, was found dead in the Arkansas river road, sixteen miles below Little Rock. Venable started late in the evening to ride from England to Little Rock on horseback, and it is supposed that he fell off his horse while asleep. His neck was broken and his ankle badly wrenched. The left stirrup on his saddle was broken. The horse he was riding was found grazing a short distance from the body.

White Boys and Negroes Fight.

A difficulty occurred between some negroes and white boys at Russellville, resulting in fatal injury to Will Davenport. The white boys made the negroes leave the depot platform and followed them some distance. The negroes then turned on the whites and began to use their knives. Clarence Montgomery, white, was also badly cut.
